articles.title: Person-to-merchant UPI payments over Rs 2,000 to attract MDR : What remains free, what will come under MDR and other things to know
articles.summary: Tech News News: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has introduced a 0.4% fee on person-to-merchant transactions exceeding Rs 2,000. Called Merchant Dis.
articles.body: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has introduced a 0.4% fee on person-to-merchant transactions exceeding Rs 2,000. Called Merchant Discount Rate (MDR), it is a charge that a merchant pays to a bank or payment service provider for processing a digital payment. Introduced under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, the new MDR provision will come into effect from October 15, 2026. In an official press release, the government clarified that the new UPI framework will have “no impact on any person to person transactions”. “UPI will continue to remain completely free for all person-to-person transactions, irrespective of the amount transferred,” the release said. Instead, “the framework seeks to ensure the long-term sustainability of UPI while protecting individuals and small merchants from additional charges,” it stated.With the new framework coming into force next month, here’s what the government said about what UPI payments remain free, what has been included under the MDR provisions and whether UPI apps will start charging platform fees on UPI payments.MDR on Person-to-merchant UPI payments above Rs 2,000: What will remain freeAll Person-to-Person Transactions: All person-to-person (P2P) UPI transactions will remain completely free, irrespective of the amount transferred. No transaction fee, platform fee or other charge may be imposed on individuals for sending or receiving money through UPI. Therefore, UPI transactions accounting for 70% of the total transaction value will remain completely outside the MDR framework.Merchant Payments Up to Rs 2,000: All person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions up to Rs 2,000 will remain free of MDR. Customers will not be required to pay any charge when making such payments through UPI.Payments Received by Small Merchants: Small merchants including street vendors receiving up to Rs 1 lakh per month through UPI QR codes under the Person-to-Person-Merchant (P2PM) category will continue to enjoy zero MDR on all transactions. This provision will protect street vendors, neighbourhood shops and other small businesses from additional payment costs.MDR on Person-to-merchant UPI payments above Rs 2,000: What will attract MDRMerchant Transactions Above Rs 2,000: A nominal MDR of 0.4% will apply only to P2M transactions above Rs 2,000. The MDR will be shared among payment ecosystem participants, including banks, payment service providers and UPI application providers. For transactions of Rs 75,000 and above, the MDR will be capped at Rs 300 per transaction.Transactions in Essential Sectors: Transactions above Rs 2,000 in essential and thin-margin sectors, including railways, telecommunications, insurance, fuel and agricultural inputs, will attract a flat MDR of Rs 5 per transaction. The flat charge will provide cost certainty for critical public services and businesses operating on narrow margins.Capital Market Transactions: Payments relating to mutual funds, securities, stockbrokers and dealers will attract an MDR of 0.02%, capped at Rs 300 per transaction. The lower rate is intended to support continued retail participation in formal financial markets.MDR on Person-to-merchant UPI payments above Rs 2,000: Customers will not pay MDRMDR is a charge within the merchant payment ecosystem. It is not a charge on customers making UPI payments. In its official announcement, the government said that banks have been advised to ensure that merchants do not pass MDR charges on to customers. UPI application providers are expressly prohibited from imposing platform fees or hidden charges.Individuals will continue to have unlimited free usage, with no monthly quotas, volume restrictions or tiered caps on free UPI transactions. Daily transaction limits prescribed by banks and NPCI, generally ranging from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 5 lakh depending on the transaction category, are security and risk-management safeguards. They are not charging thresholds.MDR on Person-to-merchant UPI payments above Rs 2,000: Most merchant transactions will remain unaffectedData analysis indicates that MDR will apply to only about 4% of merchant transactions. This means that approximately 96% of merchant transactions will remain unaffected, as they are either below the Rs 2,000 threshold or covered by the zero-MDR framework for small merchants.The framework therefore protects individuals, micro-enterprises and small businesses while introducing a limited charge on larger merchant transactions.When do the updated MDR provisions take effectThe finalized MDR framework and threshold structure take effect from 15th October 2026. This timeline gives acquiring banks, payment aggregators, fintech applications, and corporate accounting platforms adequate lead time to update their software engines and billing systems.Will small-value UPI transactions be impactedThere is no impact on small-value UPI transactions up to Rs 2,000, which comprise more than 95% of the total volume of UPI (P2M) transactions. The intent of levying reasonable MDR is to ensure that UPI remains, accessible and convenient for everyday transactions while supporting long-term ecosystem sustainability.Will UPI apps start charging platform fee on UPI paymentsNo, UPI App providers shall NOT charge Platform Fee or any other charge for any payment made through UPI. UPI applications are explicitly restricted from levying platform fees on UPI transactions.Will I need to pay a fee when scanning a QR code at a local vendorNo, scanning QR codes at local markets, street vendors, or small retail shops will remain completely free for consumers. The customer-facing side of a QR transaction involves zero fees, regardless of the purchase amount. The policy has been engineered to protect daily micro-purchases like tea stalls, and local transport from any cost burden. Consumers can continue scanning QR codes with total confidence that no extra charge will be deducted.Do small merchants need to upgrade or change their existing QR codesNo. Existing QR infrastructure will continue to function normally. Merchants do not need to replace, re-register, or alter their existing physical QR stands or soundboxes. All UPI QR codes currently displayed across shops will continue to process payments without interruption. Merchants can receive customer payments through their existing setups without visiting a bank branch or updating software.What happens if a small merchant receives a payment above Rs 2,000MDR applicability is determined by overall merchant account categorisation. Receiving a payment above Rs 2,000 does not impose a charge on a small merchant operating under exempted tiers like P2PM. A MDR of 0.4% will be introduced on Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above Rs 2,000/-. For transactions of Rs 75,000/- and above, the MDR will be capped at Rs 300 per transaction.UPI AutoPay: No prescribed MDR chargesThe government says that recurring payments made through UPI Mandates or AutoPay—such as utility bills, OTT subscriptions and mutual fund subscriptions—do not carry prescribed MDR transaction charges. Hence, they will continue to remain free of any fees.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.body: Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce have stepped up security at their new Ohio mansion to keep the nosy neighbours away from their new Ohio property. If gotten too close, the person shall receive a voice warning telling them not to enter. According to a Page-Six report, the newlyweds bought the 21,000-square-foot lakefront estate in Bratenahl for $5.35 million in March.The eight-bedroom, 11-bathroom mansion sits along Lake Erie and is among the couple’s growing list of properties. The security measures come as the area prepares for increased attention following the couple’s move.Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s Ohio mansionThe Bratenahl property offers extensive space and privacy. It has eight bedrooms and 11 bathrooms, along with a game room and a private theatre.The mansion is located in a relatively secluded lakefront community, several miles from Kelce’s childhood home in Cleveland Heights.A neighbour recently approached the property and received an automated warning after getting too close to the house.“A neighbor approached the house and got a voice warning about not passing onto the property after getting too close to the house,” a nearby neighbour told Page Six.It is not clear whether the warning system covers the entire property or was installed specifically around the mansion.Patricia Knight Gary, a veteran local realtor with Howard Hanna Realty, said she was not aware of any new fencing being installed across the village.“The village is a relatively secluded lakefront property. Something may have been set up at that particular home which is their private estate, but in terms of any additional fencing for the village, I’m not aware of that,” Knight Gary told Page Six.Police already patrol the areaBratenahl already has security measures in place, with a small police force regularly patrolling the village. Nearby condominiums also have round-the-clock security.“It does have a small police force that gauge and patrol the village on a regular basis,” Knight Gary said. “And then even at the condos [down the street], there is 24-hour security, so I would anticipate that there might be some discussion in terms of increasing that.”The arrival of Swift and Kelce could therefore bring additional security arrangements, although no wider changes have been confirmed.When did Swift and Kelce buy the house?Swift and Kelce purchased the Ohio mansion in March for $5.35 million. The purchase came before they married in July at Madison Square Garden.Despite the high-profile move, the couple have not caused any major disruption in the neighbourhood so far, according to Page Six.The property is also not expected to become their main residence.Kelce's Leawood, Kansas, home remains their primary base while he continues playing for the Kansas City Chiefs, according to a source cited by Page Six.Swift also owns properties in Nashville, Rhode Island and Beverly Hills, as well as a Tribeca apartment.“So they have plenty of options depending on where they need to be,” the source said.Neighbours expect more attentionLocal residents are now waiting to see how the celebrity couple’s arrival affects the quiet community.“We found out publicly when everyone else did (about their move),” Knight Gary said.She added, “We’re waiting to see what impact this will have in terms of the additional traffic, additional people, and the village, but I think we certainly understand that this is not their full-time home either, so we have no way of knowing at this point just what the impact will be. It’s almost a wait and see, quite frankly.”The new celebrity residents could also affect local property prices. Knight Gary said some homeowners may hope the couple’s presence increases the value of properties in the area.“I would think that certainly the residents and those who are selling would certainly have some hope that this might do something to increase values, but it is very difficult to gauge and anticipate it at this point.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Army chief General Dhiraj Seth to visit Russia in a bid to strengthen defence cooperation
articles.summary: News News: Army chief General Dhiraj Seth arrived in Russia on Wednesday for a three-day official visit running until September 18, the first by a serving Indian.
articles.body: Army chief General Dhiraj Seth arrived in Russia on Wednesday for a three-day official visit running until September 18, the first by a serving Indian Army chief to the country since General Bipin Rawat's trip back in October 2018. During the visit, Gen Seth is expected to receive a ceremonial Guard of Honour in Moscow and pay tribute at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, before holding talks with Colonel General Andrei Mordvichev, Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Land Forces, on professional military cooperation and training. This is General Seth had earlier visited Nepal last month, a country where the Indian army chief is given the honorary rank of General in its own army.Gen Seth will also visit the National Defence Control Centre and meet senior Russian Ministry of Defence officials, including Deputy Minister Vasily Osmakov, who oversees defence industry and procurement, discussions expected to touch on contemporary military developments and avenues for deeper cooperation between the armies of the two countries. From Moscow, General Seth is scheduled to visit the Mikhailovskaya Military Artillery Academy located in Saint Petersburg.One of the central issues on the table is spare parts and sustainment support for Russian-origin equipment in service across the Indian Army, from assault rifles to tanks and air defence systems, with almost the entire Armoured Corps and Mechanised Infantry still dependent on Russian origin platforms even as India seeks to largely indigenise its military equipment. Russia has also offered newer systems, such as the Pantsir-S1M air defence system and the latest variant of the BMP-3, alongside proposals for India's Future Ready Combat Vehicle programme meant to eventually replace the T-72 and T-90 tank fleets. India has also co-developed the Brahmos missile with the Russians. Russia has also been pitching the Su-57 fifth generation fighter and the S-500 air defence system to India.The visit lands amid a much broader web of ongoing engagement. The relationship has evolved from a buyer-seller arrangement into joint production, with the T-90 and Su-30 MKI already built in India, and INS Tamal, a stealth frigate, commissioned at Kaliningrad this July. Institutional talks continued through Working Group meetings in New Delhi and Moscow in October, while military exercises stayed active too, of INDRA in Bikaner, Indian participation in Russia's Zapad-2025 drills, a separate naval INDRA exercise across Chennai and the Bay of Bengal, and an air exercise in Thanjavur in December, underscoring how layered this defence relationship remains even as India recalibrates its broader strategic alignments.

articles.title: At 20, a college student became mayor of an Iowa town with just 144 people; she may be America's youngest mayor
articles.summary: US News: Eva Fipps stepped into local government at an age when many people are still deciding what they want to study or do after college. At 20, she became m.
articles.body: Eva Fipps stepped into local government at an age when many people are still deciding what they want to study or do after college. At 20, she became mayor of Henderson, a small town in southwest Iowa with 144 residents. Her election has drawn attention because she may be the youngest serving mayor in the United States. Yet behind the unusual age is a practical story about a young resident becoming involved in her community, learning the responsibilities of public office and trying to give a very small town new kind of energy.20-year-old college student becoming the mayor of HendersonFipps did not begin with a long-term plan to become mayor. According to Radio Iowa, she regularly went for runs or walks with her dogs and would stop at Henderson City Hall to talk with city clerk Candace Knop. Their conversations had continued for years, including during the COVID period.Knop eventually suggested that Fipps should consider running for mayor. Fipps had not seriously considered the idea because of her age, but she decided that taking part in the election could still be worthwhile even if she did not win. Radio Iowa reported that she viewed the experience as an opportunity to learn about local government.That decision led to an election in November 2025. Fipps defeated Scott Schondelmeyer by 30 votes, according to Radio Iowa. She was later sworn into office on 29 December, beginning a new chapter for the college student.What was so unique about her electionHenderson's size makes the result particularly distinctive. KCCI reported that the Mills County town has 144 residents, meaning Fipps is serving a community small enough for local politics to remain closely connected to everyday life.Her age has also placed her among a small group of young elected officials in the area. KCCI reported that Mills County had another young officeholder, a 19-year-old county supervisor Jack Sayers, while 21-year-old Joseph Jaworkski had been elected mayor of nearby Silver City.Y105 reported Fipps as possibly the youngest mayor in the United States and potentially the youngest female mayor in the country's history. She was sworn in at the beginning of January 2026.Fipps brought early public service experience into officeAlthough she was new to the mayor's position, Fipps had already gained experience in public affairs before seeking the office. Radio Iowa reported that she graduated from Treynor High School in 2024 and had been a dual enrollee at Iowa Western Community College.She also took part in Iowa Girls State and served as a page in the Iowa Legislature. Those experiences gave her an early introduction to how government works and helped shape her interest in public service. Y105 reported that Fipps has ambitions of attending law school. For now, however, her attention is centred on Henderson and the responsibilities that came with becoming its mayor.What does the new mayor want to change in HendersonFipps has identified several practical goals for the town rather than focusing only on the novelty surrounding her age. Radio Iowa reported that she wants to encourage greater community involvement and organise more activities that could bring current residents, former residents and people from surrounding communities together.She also wants to address some of Henderson's empty shopfronts and renovate the town's playground. These plans reflect the everyday challenges facing a very small community, where maintaining shared spaces and attracting activity can be important parts of keeping the town active.Fipps is learning the responsibilities of local governmentThe transition has involved a learning curve. Radio Iowa reported that Fipps was preparing to take a class on open meetings, which would help her understand her responsibilities and how to carry them out properly.She has also been speaking with other mayors, city clerks and board members as she learns the details of the position. Radio Iowa reported that much of her early work has involved communication and absorbing information from people with more experience in local government.For a 20-year-old who is still pursuing her education, becoming mayor means balancing an unusual set of responsibilities. Her election has attracted attention because of her age, but the early stages of her term are centred on familiar local-government tasks such as understanding procedures, working with officials and responding to community needs.What could Fipps represent for the small Iowa townFipps's arrival also adds another young voice to local government in Mills County. For Henderson, the immediate focus is less about national attention and more about what can happen within a community of 144 people.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: International News: Japan is moving to develop compact quantum magnetic sensors that can be mounted on small drones to detect submarines underwater, as Tokyo looks to exp.
articles.body: Japan is moving to develop compact quantum magnetic sensors that can be mounted on small drones to detect submarines underwater, as Tokyo looks to expand its anti-submarine surveillance capabilities amid growing Chinese naval activity in the Indo-Pacific.According to the Nikkei newspaper, the project has been included in Japan’s fiscal 2027 defence budget request, with the defence ministry targeting completion of development by fiscal 2031.The planned system would use low-cost drones flying close to the sea surface from warships to detect tiny changes in the Earth’s magnetic field caused by submerged vessels. The Japanese government has positioned the technology as part of its wider push to use unmanned systems to make underwater threats more visible while reducing reliance on crewed platforms.How the technology worksAccording to the South China Morning Post, Japan’s planned system will use a quantum magnetic sensor to detect tiny changes in the magnetic field that could indicate the presence of a submarine. The sensor uses the properties of atoms to make highly sensitive magnetic measurements.Nato's Science and Technology Organization says magnetic anomaly detection sensors are already used to help locate submarines, but conventional systems are too large and power-hungry for small UAVs. It says newer quantum magnetic sensors could overcome some of these limitations.In simple terms, the drone would fly over the sea and look for unusual changes in the magnetic field below it. A detected anomaly could indicate a submarine, which can then be investigated using other anti-submarine warfare systems.How the sensor will be used on dronesJapan plans to put the quantum magnetic sensor on a small, low-cost drone that can operate close to the sea surface. According to the South China Morning Post, the drones could be launched from warships and used to search for submarines without putting a crewed aircraft at risk.The main advantage is the possibility of using many inexpensive drones instead of relying only on larger, crewed aircraft. Each drone could carry the sensor over a designated area and send information about any detected magnetic anomaly back to the Japanese forces.ImplicationsThe biggest advantage for Japan would be the ability to deploy a large number of relatively cheap drones to monitor areas where Chinese submarines may pass. Experts told South China Morning Post that the limited range of magnetic sensing makes such systems more useful around narrow waterways and straits rather than across vast areas of ocean.The drones could add another layer to Japan's anti-submarine warfare network, working alongside maritime patrol aircraft, ships, sonar and other sensors. This could allow Japan to keep watch over important sea routes for longer without relying entirely on expensive crewed aircraft.The development also comes as China expands its own use of quantum sensing for military applications. Chinese researchers have reported testing a drone-mounted quantum magnetic sensor at sea, suggesting that underwater detection could become another area of competition between the two countries.

articles.title: India, Pakistani naval ships collide in international waters; MEA calls conduct 'unprofessional'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday summoned Pakistan’s top diplomat in New Delhi and lodged a strong protest over the “unacceptable and unprofessional cond.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday summoned Pakistan’s top diplomat in New Delhi and lodged a strong protest over the “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct” of Pakistani naval units that led to a collision with an Indian Navy vessel in international waters.“While the incident, which took place in international waters, did not cause any major damage, the conduct of the Pakistani naval ship was in direct contravention of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991,” the MEA said in a statement.The ministry said the Pakistani Charge d’Affaires was advised to convey to the concerned authorities that all military units must exercise due care and comply with relevant agreements between the two countries.“The Charge d'Affaires of Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents,” it said.The MEA also said India’s Charge d’Affaires in Islamabad had been instructed to lodge a similar protest with Pakistan’s ministry of foreign affairs.This is not the first time Indian and Pakistani ships have come into close contact in the Arabian Sea.In 2011, a diplomatic row had erupted over the MV Suez episode, then Navy chief Admiral Nirmal Verma said Pakistani warship PNS Babur had come “much closer” than was prudent, damaging a helicopter net on INS Godavari. He said the Indian crew had acted “very professionally” and stressed that “there are clear rules of navigation at sea”.What the 1991 agreement saysThe 1991 India-Pakistan agreement lays down rules for advance notice of major military exercises, manoeuvres and troop movements.Under the agreement, the land, naval and air forces of both countries are to avoid major exercises close to each other. If such exercises are conducted within specified areas, the main force cannot be directed towards the other side and there should be no logistical build-up close to it.For land forces, exercises involving a division or larger formation are restricted within 5 km of specified areas along the International Border, Line of Control and the area between the Manawar Tawi and Ravi rivers. The agreement also requires advance notice for division-level exercises in designated areas, corps-level exercises within 75 km, and all exercises above corps level regardless of distance.For naval forces, an exercise involving six or more destroyer- or frigate-sized ships crossing into the other country's EEZ is covered. Air-force exercises at regional command level or above also fall under the agreement.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Finland's coast is still rising after the Ice Age; around the Gulf of Bothnia, 1,730 acres emerge each year, but waterfront owners may not own the new land

articles.body: For thousands of years, Finland’s western shoreline has been quietly changing shape. Ground that was once pressed beneath an enormous sheet of ice is still rising, pushing parts of the coast farther out into the Gulf of Bothnia. To the eye, the process can look like nature simply adding more land. For waterfront property owners, however, the reality is more complicated: newly exposed ground does not automatically become an extension of the property behind it. According to an online report by ECONews, during the last ice age, the enormous weight of the Scandinavian ice sheet pushed the land downward by more than 500 meters in parts of the region. When the ice retreated more than 10,000 years ago, the Earth's crust began a slow rebound. The process, known as post-glacial rebound, continues today.According to the news, Finland’s National Land Survey says the fastest uplift occurs around Kvarken, where the land rises by almost one centimeter a year. In southeastern Finland, the rate is less than three millimeters annually. NASA estimates that around the Gulf of Bothnia, about 700 hectares, or roughly 1,730 acres, of land emerges from the water each year. The figure gives a sense of the scale of the transformation, although it does not mean an individual property is gaining land at anything close to that rate. And the National Land Survey estimates that as much as another 100 meters of uplift could still occur near the Gulf of Bothnia.New land does not automatically belong to the nearest ownerThe legal situation becomes particularly interesting when the rising ground appears directly in front of a waterfront property. In Finland, land that was once covered by water but has become dry is known as vesijättö, commonly translated into English as a reliction area. It can form because of land uplift, falling water levels or the gradual overgrowth of waterways. The ownership of that land does not automatically shift to the person whose property happens to sit closest to it. In many cases, ownership remains with whoever owned the original water area. That can mean the newly exposed ground belongs to several property owners collectively through a jointly owned water area, often organized as an osakaskunta. In other words, the landscape can change without the property register changing with it.The shoreline can move while property boundaries stay putAccording to the report, that distinction can have practical consequences. A cottage that once stood directly beside the water may eventually have a stretch of dry land between its boundary and the shoreline. The owner may still have the same property they always had, even though the coast looks very different. Finland’s National Land Survey makes clear that natural changes do not automatically alter property boundaries. The location of the waterline is therefore not, by itself, proof of who owns the ground between a property and the sea. The issue is hardly new. Records from Östhammar, Sweden, describe complaints dating back to 1491, when the retreat of the shoreline had made the town’s old harbor unusable.Owners can seek to acquire the emerging landWaterfront owners are not necessarily left without an option. An eligible property owner can apply to acquire adjacent reliction land through a formal redemption process administered by the National Land Survey. A surveyor assesses whether the land qualifies, determines its value and establishes the compensation to be paid. Once the process is completed, the resulting information is recorded in the property register. The agency estimates that the procedure takes around seven months, although individual cases can take longer. Winter conditions can also delay fieldwork. There are costs involved. Current guidance puts the average procedural cost for a cottage plot at roughly €2,000 to €3,000. That amount covers the procedure itself and does not include compensation to the existing landowner or any applicable taxes.A changing coast requires a closer look at the property lineFor people living along Finland’s western coast, the lesson is straightforward. A changing shoreline does not necessarily mean a changing property boundary. Before building a dock, extending a yard or carrying out other work on newly exposed ground, property owners need to establish exactly where their legal boundary lies and whether a reliction area exists in front of it. The broader geological story also comes with an important qualification. Rising land is not the same thing as falling sea levels. Future changes along the Gulf of Bothnia will depend partly on how continued land uplift interacts with rising global sea levels.For now, Finland offers a striking example of how slowly moving geology can have very practical consequences. The ice age may be long gone, but its effects are still reshaping the coastline, and creating new questions about where nature ends and property ownership begins.Image Courtesy: ECONewsCatch the latest World News and Live updates.
